prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We systematically explore the evolution of the merger of two carbon-oxygen (CO) white dwarfs. The dynamical evolution of a 0.9 Msun + 0.6 Msun CO white dwarf merger is followed by a three-dimensional SPH simulation. We use an elaborate prescription in which artificial viscosity is essentially absent, unless a shock is detected, and a much larger number of SPH particles than earlier calculations. Based on this simulation, we suggest that the central region of the merger remnant can, once it has reached quasi-static equilibrium, be approximated as a differentially rotating CO star, which consists of a slowly rotating cold core and a rapidly rotating hot envelope surrounded by a centrifugally supported disc. We construct a model of the CO remnant that mimics the results of the SPH simulation using a one-dimensional hydrodynamic stellar evolution code and then follow its secular evolution. The stellar evolution models indicate that the growth of the cold core is controlled by neutrino cooling at the interface between the core and the hot envelope, and that carbon ignition in the envelope can be avoided despite high effective accretion rates. This result suggests that the assumption of forced accretion of cold matter that was adopted in previous studies of the evolution of double CO white dwarf merger remnants may not be appropriate. Our results imply that at least some products of double CO white dwarfs merger may be considered good candidates for the progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. In this case, the characteristic time delay between the initial dynamical merger and the eventual explosion would be ~10^5 yr. (Abridged).

outputs.L1:
We systematically investigate the evolution of a merger between two carbon–oxygen (CO) white dwarfs. The dynamical evolution of a 0.9 M⊙ + 0.6 M⊙ CO white dwarf merger is followed using a three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation. We adopt an elaborate prescription in which artificial viscosity is essentially absent except when a shock is detected, and we employ a substantially larger number of SPH particles than in earlier calculations.

On the basis of this simulation, we suggest that, once the central region of the merger remnant has reached quasi-static equilibrium, it can be approximated as a differentially rotating CO star composed of a slowly rotating cold core and a rapidly rotating hot envelope, surrounded by a centrifugally supported disc. We construct a model of the CO remnant that reproduces the results of the SPH simulation using a one-dimensional hydrodynamic stellar evolution code, and then follow its secular evolution.

The stellar evolution models indicate that the growth of the cold core is governed by neutrino cooling at the interface between the core and the hot envelope, and that carbon ignition in the envelope can be avoided despite high effective accretion rates. This result suggests that the forced accretion of cold matter assumed in previous studies of the evolution of double CO white dwarf merger remnants may not be appropriate.

Our results imply that at least some products of double CO white dwarf mergers may be viable candidates for the progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. In this scenario, the characteristic time delay between the initial dynamical merger and the eventual explosion would be approximately 10^5 yr. (Abridged)
outputs.L2:
We investigate in detail how a merger between two carbon–oxygen (CO) white dwarfs develops over time. The dynamical phase of a merger involving CO white dwarfs of 0.9 \(M_\odot\) and 0.6 \(M_\odot\) is modeled with a three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation. Our calculation employs a refined treatment in which artificial viscosity is effectively switched off except when shocks are identified, and it uses far more SPH particles than earlier studies.

Using the simulation results, we propose that after the merger remnant settles into a quasi-static state, its central region can be represented as a differentially rotating CO star. This object is made up of a cold, slowly spinning core and a hot envelope rotating much more rapidly, with the whole structure surrounded by a disc supported by centrifugal forces. To reproduce the SPH outcome, we build a corresponding CO-remnant model with a one-dimensional hydrodynamic stellar evolution code and then track its long-term evolution.

The stellar evolution calculations show that expansion of the cold core is regulated by neutrino cooling at the boundary between the core and the hot envelope. They also indicate that carbon ignition in the envelope can be prevented, even when the effective accretion rates are large. This finding implies that the earlier assumption, used in studies of double CO white dwarf merger remnants, that cold material is forcibly accreted may not be valid.

Overall, our results suggest that at least some remnants produced by mergers of two CO white dwarfs could be plausible progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. In such a scenario, the expected delay between the initial dynamical merger and the final supernova explosion would be approximately \(10^5\) years. This is an abridged summary.
outputs.L3:
The study investigates the evolution of a merger between two carbon-oxygen white dwarfs with masses of 0.9 solar masses and 0.6 solar masses. To follow the merger process, the authors use a three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation, which allows them to model the complex dynamics of the disruption, mass transfer, and remnant formation in detail.

After the merger, the remnant is approximated as a differentially rotating carbon-oxygen star. Its structure consists of three main regions: a relatively cold central core, a much hotter envelope surrounding the core, and an outer disc that is supported partly by centrifugal forces. This configuration reflects the outcome of the violent merger process, in which the less massive white dwarf is disrupted and its material is redistributed around the more massive primary.

The subsequent long-term evolution of the remnant is studied using one-dimensional stellar evolution models. These models show that the cold core grows over time. This growth is driven by neutrino cooling near the interface between the cold core and the hot envelope. As the interface cools, material from the envelope is incorporated into the core, gradually increasing its mass.

An important result of the models is that carbon ignition in the envelope can be avoided, even though the effective accretion rates onto the core are high. In many scenarios, such high accretion rates would be expected to trigger off-centre carbon burning, potentially leading to the formation of an oxygen-neon remnant rather than a Type Ia supernova. However, in this case, the cooling and thermal structure of the merger remnant prevent carbon from igniting prematurely in the envelope.

These findings suggest that at least some mergers of double carbon-oxygen white dwarfs may remain viable progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. If the remnant continues to evolve without off-centre carbon ignition, it may eventually reach conditions suitable for a thermonuclear explosion. The estimated delay time between the merger event and the possible supernova explosion is approximately \(10^5\) years.
outputs.L4:
This study examines the long-term fate of a merger between two carbon-oxygen white dwarfs with masses of 0.9 and 0.6 solar masses. The merger phase is followed using high-resolution three-dimensional smoothed-particle hydrodynamics simulations. These simulations incorporate an improved, shock-dependent artificial viscosity prescription, allowing the hydrodynamical interaction, heating, and angular-momentum redistribution during the merger to be modeled more accurately than in lower-resolution or more diffusive calculations.

The simulations show that the less massive white dwarf is disrupted and forms a hot, rapidly rotating envelope around the more massive primary, while a relatively cold, degenerate core survives at the center of the remnant. The resulting structure is not immediately explosive. Instead, it consists of a dense central core surrounded by hot carbon-oxygen material, with thermal and compositional profiles that determine its later evolution.

To follow this later stage, the three-dimensional merger remnant is mapped into a one-dimensional stellar evolution calculation. This allows the study to track the secular evolution of the object over much longer timescales than can be simulated directly in three dimensions. Particular attention is paid to the competition between compressional heating, carbon burning, angular-momentum transport, and neutrino cooling.

A key result is that neutrino cooling plays a decisive role in the thermal evolution of the remnant. By removing energy from the hot envelope and from regions near the core-envelope boundary, neutrino emission regulates the growth of the cold central core. This cooling can prevent carbon from igniting in the hot envelope shortly after the merger. Such off-center carbon ignition would otherwise likely convert the remnant into an oxygen-neon object, making it less likely to produce a normal Type Ia supernova.

Instead, if envelope carbon ignition is avoided, the cold degenerate core can continue to grow in mass as material is processed and added to it. The remnant may then evolve toward conditions suitable for carbon ignition near the center. In this scenario, the merger does not produce an immediate explosion, but rather forms a delayed Type Ia supernova progenitor.

The study therefore suggests that at least some mergers of double carbon-oxygen white dwarfs, including systems with total masses near the Chandrasekhar mass, may survive the initial dynamical phase and later explode after a secular delay. For the 0.9 solar-mass plus 0.6 solar-mass system considered here, the delay time is estimated to be on the order of \(10^5\) years. This finding highlights the importance of accurate treatment of shocks during the merger and of neutrino cooling during the post-merger evolution when assessing whether double white dwarf mergers can lead to Type Ia supernovae.
outputs.L5:
**The Role of SPH in Simulating Objects Measured in Msun**

The study of astrophysical systems often requires modeling objects with masses expressed in **Msun**, or solar masses. One Msun is equal to the mass of the Sun and is commonly used to describe stars, gas clouds, black holes, and entire galaxies. For example, a massive star may have a mass of 20 Msun, while a giant molecular cloud can contain thousands or even millions of Msun of gas.

One important numerical method used to study these systems is **SPH**, which stands for **Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics**. SPH is a computational technique that represents fluids as a collection of particles. Each particle carries properties such as mass, velocity, density, and temperature. This makes SPH especially useful in astrophysics, where gas flows can be highly complex and three-dimensional.

Using SPH, scientists can simulate events such as star formation, galaxy collisions, supernova explosions, and accretion around black holes. The method allows researchers to follow how gas with many Msun of material moves, collapses, heats, and forms new structures over time.

The combination of Msun as a unit of mass and SPH as a simulation method helps astronomers better understand the behavior of matter in the universe. Through these tools, complex cosmic processes can be studied in detail, even when they occur far beyond the reach of direct observation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a paper on 3D SPH simulations of a 0.9 + 0.6 solar mass carbon-oxygen white dwarf merger and its implications for Type Ia supernova progenitors.
counterfactuals.output: We present three-dimensional smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations of the merger of a 0.9 + 0.6 M_\(\odot\) carbon–oxygen white dwarf binary, a system relevant to the double-degenerate channel for Type Ia supernova progenitors. The calculation follows the onset of dynamical mass transfer, tidal disruption of the lower-mass secondary, and formation of a hot accretion flow around the more massive primary. We characterize the thermodynamic structure, angular-momentum distribution, mixing, and peak temperatures reached during the merger, with particular attention to whether conditions are favorable for prompt carbon ignition or subsequent delayed detonation after viscous evolution. Our results show that the secondary is rapidly disrupted and forms an extended, differentially rotating envelope and disk surrounding a relatively intact primary. Although localized heating occurs in the shear layer and accretion stream impact region, the peak densities and temperatures during the dynamical phase remain below those generally required for robust prompt detonation in this mass combination. The remnant therefore appears more likely to undergo further secular evolution, including angular-momentum redistribution, compressional heating, and possible off-center carbon ignition. These outcomes suggest that 0.9 + 0.6 M_\(\odot\) carbon–oxygen white dwarf mergers may contribute to the diversity of thermonuclear transients, but are unlikely to produce normal Type Ia supernovae through a prompt dynamical detonation alone. Our simulations provide constraints on the viability of sub-Chandrasekhar and near-Chandrasekhar double-degenerate progenitor pathways and highlight the importance of coupling high-resolution hydrodynamic merger calculations to long-term thermal and viscous evolution models.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of a study modeling the merger of two CO white dwarfs, including the SPH simulation setup, remnant structure, secular evolution, and carbon ignition outcome.
counterfactuals.output:
The study followed the merger of two carbon–oxygen white dwarfs and then evolved the merger product on longer, secular timescales. Its main conclusion was that the modeled merger does **not** naturally produce a prompt Type Ia supernova; instead, it forms a differentially rotating remnant that later undergoes **off-center carbon ignition**, likely leading to conversion into an ONe white dwarf and possible accretion-induced collapse if it approaches the Chandrasekhar mass.

### 1. SPH merger simulation setup

- The merger was modeled with a 3D smoothed-particle hydrodynamics, or SPH, calculation.
- The binary consisted of two CO white dwarfs, typically a more massive primary and a lower-mass secondary, e.g. a system like \(0.9\,M_\odot + 0.6\,M_\odot\).
- Both stars were initialized as cold or moderately warm CO white dwarfs in a close binary orbit.
- The lower-mass white dwarf was tidally disrupted as mass transfer became dynamically unstable.
- The calculation followed the dynamical merger phase over several orbital periods.

The SPH simulation found no robust prompt carbon detonation during the merger for the modeled system. Temperatures rose substantially in shocks and shear layers, but not in a way that produced an immediate thermonuclear runaway.

### 2. Structure of the merger remnant

The remnant had a characteristic three-component structure:

1. **Cold central core**  
   - Mostly the original primary white dwarf.
   - Degenerate and relatively cool compared with the surrounding material.

2. **Hot, pressure-supported envelope/corona**  
   - Formed from disrupted material from the secondary.
   - Reached the highest temperatures.
   - Rotated differentially and contained a large fraction of the thermal energy.

3. **Rotationally supported disk**  
   - Extended to larger radii.
   - Contained the remaining disrupted secondary material.
   - Served as a reservoir for later accretion onto the central remnant.

The remnant was strongly differentially rotating, with angular momentum concentrated in the outer envelope and disk.

### 3. Secular evolution after the merger

Because the SPH calculation only follows the dynamical phase, the remnant was mapped into a one-dimensional or quasi-one-dimensional stellar evolution model to follow its longer-term evolution.

The secular evolution was controlled by:

- angular momentum transport,
- viscous dissipation,
- thermal diffusion,
- neutrino cooling,
- nuclear burning,
- accretion from the disk onto the core.

As angular momentum was redistributed, the disk and envelope material accreted inward. Viscous heating raised the temperature near the interface between the cold core and the hot envelope. The remnant expanded somewhat, but the base of the accreted layer became hot and dense enough for carbon burning.

### 4. Carbon ignition outcome

The key result was that carbon ignited **off-center**, not at the center.

- The ignition occurred near the core-envelope interface, where accreted material was compressed and heated.
- The burning was not explosive in the modeled case.
- Instead, it developed into a relatively stable carbon-burning flame.
- This flame would propagate inward, converting the CO material into an oxygen–neon, or ONe, composition.

Thus, rather than producing a normal Type Ia supernova through central carbon ignition, the remnant was expected to become an ONe white dwarf. If its mass remained near or above the Chandrasekhar mass, subsequent electron captures could trigger collapse to a neutron star, i.e. accretion-induced collapse, rather than thermonuclear disruption.

### Overall conclusion

The study found that a CO white dwarf merger can leave behind a massive, differentially rotating remnant with a cold core, hot envelope, and disk. Its long-term viscous evolution drives accretion and heating that lead to **off-center carbon ignition**. For the modeled system, this favors formation of an ONe remnant and possible collapse, not a prompt or ordinary Type Ia supernova.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an astronomy journal-style abstract about the evolution of double carbon-oxygen white dwarf merger remnants, emphasizing neutrino cooling, differential rotation, and delayed Type Ia supernova explosions.
counterfactuals.output:
We present evolutionary models for merger remnants produced by double carbon–oxygen white dwarf coalescence, focusing on the thermodynamic pathways that regulate their fate as potential Type Ia supernova progenitors. The post-merger configuration consists of a cold, degenerate primary surrounded by a hot, differentially rotating envelope and a rotationally supported disk. We follow the coupled evolution of thermal structure, angular momentum redistribution, and composition under the influence of neutrino cooling, viscous dissipation, and compressional heating. Neutrino losses efficiently cool the hottest envelope layers and shift the temperature maximum inward, modifying the conditions for carbon ignition relative to purely adiabatic or viscously heated models. Differential rotation initially provides substantial centrifugal support and delays central compression; however, angular momentum transport gradually drives the remnant toward a more compact state, increasing central density and temperature on secular timescales.

Our results indicate that the competition between neutrino cooling and rotationally mediated contraction determines whether carbon burning ignites off-center, leading to conversion into an oxygen–neon remnant and possible accretion-induced collapse, or remains delayed until near-central ignition becomes possible. In systems with sufficiently massive primaries and inefficient early off-center ignition, the remnant may survive for \(10^4\)–\(10^6\) yr before reaching conditions favorable for thermonuclear runaway. This delay provides a natural channel for Type Ia supernova explosions with extended post-merger latency, reduced circumstellar interaction, and potential observational diversity arising from remnant mass, rotation profile, and cooling history. We conclude that neutrino cooling and differential rotation are critical ingredients in assessing the viability of double-degenerate Type Ia progenitors and in predicting their delay-time distributions, ignition geometries, and nucleosynthetic outcomes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you draft an abridged abstract for a research article that follows a 0.9 Msun and 0.6 Msun CO white dwarf merger using high-resolution 3D SPH and then models the remnant with a 1D stellar evolution code?
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract**  
We present a high-resolution three-dimensional smoothed-particle hydrodynamics study of the merger of a 0.9 M\(_\odot\) and 0.6 M\(_\odot\) carbon–oxygen white dwarf binary, followed by one-dimensional stellar evolution calculations of the post-merger remnant. The hydrodynamic simulation resolves the disruption of the secondary, the formation of a differentially rotating remnant composed of a cold primary core, a hot convective envelope, and a surrounding debris disk, and the associated thermal and compositional structure produced during coalescence. We map the azimuthally averaged remnant profile into a 1D stellar evolution code to follow its subsequent viscous, thermal, and nuclear evolution. The remnant undergoes rapid thermal readjustment as angular momentum transport drives accretion from the disk/envelope onto the central object, raising temperatures in the outer core and at the core–envelope interface. We examine whether carbon ignition occurs under degenerate or non-degenerate conditions and assess the implications for the remnant’s fate, including possible collapse, thermonuclear disruption, or evolution toward a massive white dwarf. Our results highlight the importance of accurately resolving the three-dimensional merger phase and preserving the remnant’s entropy, rotation, and composition profiles when modeling long-term evolution. This combined SPH–stellar-evolution approach provides a physically motivated link between dynamical white dwarf mergers and their potential observational outcomes, including Type Ia supernovae and related transients.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a concise scientific summary of research arguing that forced accretion of cold matter is not appropriate for double CO white dwarf merger remnants and that some such remnants may become Type Ia supernovae after about 10^5 years.
counterfactuals.output:
Research on double carbon–oxygen white-dwarf merger remnants—especially the work of Yoon, Podsiadlowski, and collaborators—argues that the traditional “forced accretion of cold matter” treatment is physically inappropriate for these systems.

In older models, the disrupted secondary white dwarf was often approximated as cold material accreting rapidly onto the primary. Such calculations typically found strong compressional heating, off-centre carbon ignition, conversion to an ONeMg white dwarf, and eventual accretion-induced collapse rather than a Type Ia supernova.

Merger simulations show a different structure: the remnant is not a cold accreting white dwarf, but a hot, differentially rotating object surrounded by a thermally supported envelope or disk made from the disrupted companion. Because the accreted material has high entropy and significant angular momentum, its subsequent evolution is governed by thermal relaxation, angular-momentum transport, and viscous heating—not by simple cold, spherical accretion.

When these more realistic post-merger structures are evolved, some super-Chandrasekhar CO remnants avoid prompt off-centre ignition. Instead, after roughly \(10^5\) years, angular-momentum redistribution and thermal evolution can raise the central density and temperature enough for central carbon ignition. In sufficiently massive remnants, this may lead to a thermonuclear runaway and a Type Ia supernova.

Thus, the key claim is that double CO white-dwarf mergers should be modeled as hot, rotating merger remnants rather than cold accretion sequences, and that a subset of such remnants remain viable delayed Type Ia supernova progenitors on \(\sim 10^5\)-year timescales.
